Newly emergent larvae of the Greater argentine (Argentina silus) measure approximately 1.7 centimeters [Lb = approximately 1.7 centimeters] in total length at birth, a size characteristic of the pre-flexion developmental stage. At this early phase, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves, with the wet weight at birth recorded at just 0.019 grams [Wwb = 0.019 grams]. This minimal mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 3.3 mm, underscores the substantial energetic investment required for the larva to progress through the yolk absorption stage and initiate first exogenous feeding. The transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic mode is a critical bottleneck; field studies suggest that the availability of suitable planktonic prey at the moment of mouth opening strongly influences early survivorship. Within the cold, productive waters of the North Atlantic, where this species is commonly found, the preflexion and flexion-stage larvae drift as ichthyoplankton, gradually developing the fin ray ossification and body plan reorganization that will culminate in metamorphosis.

As the pelagic larva grows, it undergoes a pronounced allometric shift before settling into the juvenile phase. Females ultimately attain an asymptotic body size of approximately 70 centimeters [Li = approximately 70 centimeters] in total length, which corresponds to an ultimate female wet weight of around 3170 grams [Wwi = around 3170 grams]. This length-weight relationship, derived from extensive field surveys, places Argentina silus among the larger members of the family Argentinidae, with a body plan adapted for efficient mid-water foraging. The power-function coefficient describing this relationship aligns closely with values reported for other bathypelagic teleosts, reflecting the biomechanical constraints of sustained swimming in a viscous medium. Growth trajectories inferred from otolith microincrements indicate that the period of most rapid mass gain occurs during the first few years post-metamorphosis, after which the rate of length increase decelerates markedly as the fish approaches its ultimate size. Such asymptotic growth is a common feature of iteroparous, cold-water marine fishes.

Reproductive maturity in Argentina silus is attained when individuals reach a total length of roughly 26 centimeters [Lp = roughly 26 centimeters] at puberty, which translates to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 133 grams [Wwp = approximately 133 grams]. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is evidently size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent, a pattern frequently observed in deep-sea fishes where unpredictable food availability decouples age from somatic condition. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from specimens collected across the Scotian Shelf indicates that the initiation of vitellogenesis coincides closely with this length threshold. The delay in reproductive maturation until the fish has accumulated sufficient somatic reserves is likely an adaptive response to the energetic demands of spawning in a cold, oligotrophic environment. Pubescent individuals that have recently crossed this length threshold show developing oocytes, though they do not typically participate in the annual spawning aggregation until they have grown somewhat beyond this minimum size.

Under the stable thermal conditions of the deep-water habitat, which typically hover around 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the reproductive output of a 45-centimeter female has been estimated at approximately 32 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 32 eggs per spawning event], with a single spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = single spawning event occurring each year]. This daily egg production rate, reflecting a combination of clutch size and the protracted spawning interval typical of this species, is modest compared to that of many other marine teleosts. Field observations confirm that spawning is a single annual event, with gravid individuals aggregating over the continental slope during late winter. The relatively low fecundity per spawning event, combined with the production of large, yolk-rich pelagic eggs, suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward offspring quality rather than numerical output. These reproductive characteristics are consistent with those of other deep-water argentiniforms that experience low but stable juvenile mortality in the absence of intense predation.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Argentina silus in the wild is approximately 35 years [am = approximately 35 years], a remarkable longevity that is sustained by the cold, energy-sparing environment of its deep-sea habitat at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturation and low annual fecundity, positions the species as a classic K-selected strategist among teleosts. Senescence in these fish appears to be gradual, with the oldest individuals showing signs of reproductive senescence only after several decades of spawning activity. Comparative analyses with other members of the family Argentinidae suggest that the combination of slow growth, high ultimate body mass, and extreme longevity is a conserved trait among deep-water forms. The low metabolic costs associated with life at 7 °C likely enable this species to allocate energy to somatic maintenance and reproduction over an exceptionally protracted period. Such a life-history profile renders the Greater argentine particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as population recovery from perturbation would necessarily be very slow.

Beyond these life-history attributes, the ecological role of the Greater argentine in the North Atlantic food web merits consideration. As a mid-water planktivore, Argentina silus occupies a trophic position that links secondary production (zooplankton) to higher predators including marine mammals and large demersal fishes. Stable isotope analyses have confirmed a diet dominated by calanoid copepods and euphausiids, with occasional inclusion of small pelagic fishes. The relatively low fecundity per spawning event, producing approximately 32 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 32 eggs per spawning event], is offset by the prolonged reproductive lifespan afforded by the species' maximum age of 35 years [am = 35 years] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This combination of moderate annual egg output and extended reproductive tenure yields a lifetime fecundity that, while not exceptionally high in absolute terms, is sufficient to sustain the population under the low-mortality conditions of the deep-sea environment. Ongoing oceanographic changes affecting the temperature regime at depth, currently around 7 °C [T = 7 °C], may alter the species' metabolic costs and thereby influence its long-term population dynamics and resilience to fishing pressure.
